title: Drill a 5 mm hole through a small aluminium plate at its punch mark on a bench drill press
instruction: Drill a hole right through the aluminium plate at its punch mark with the drill press, then leave the drill switched off with its quill up. The plate must not move while it is drilled, and no part of either gripper may come within 5 cm of the bit or the chuck while they turn.
context: Drilling small parts on a bench drill press is everyday work for machinists, maintenance and repair workers and metal fabricators. A bit grabs a loose part and spins it round, a common workshop injury, so a small part is clamped before it is drilled and the hands stay clear of the turning chuck. The motor has its own switch; the quill is fed down with the capstan handle. A hold-down clamp's pad turns with its screw and twists a loose part out of place as it tightens unless the part is held. Drilling 5 mm through aluminium takes about 0.3 N m; the clamp 8 cm from the bit holds that at about 8 N of pad force (friction 0.5), and a hand-tight clamp presses about 100 N.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases, sideways from the midpoint between them, and up from the table top. (1) A fixed 8-inch (203 mm swing) bench drill press of the common 1/3 hp, five-speed class, cast iron painted blue-grey, its spindle 32 cm forward on the centre line: a 290 x 190 x 40 mm base from 15.5 to 44.5 cm forward; a 46 mm steel column 10.5 cm behind the spindle, 47 cm tall; the head 14 cm wide from 33.5 to 47.5 cm up, its front 5.5 cm ahead of the spindle, with the belt cover on top to 55.5 cm and the motor behind. A 13 mm keyed chuck (46 mm across, 76 mm long) holds a 5 mm high-speed-steel jobber drill 55 mm out of the chuck. The quill travels 50 mm, limited to 24 mm by the depth stop, against a return spring (40 N at rest, rising 530 N/m). Feed: a three-spoke capstan handle on the right of the head, its shaft 39 cm up and 2.5 cm behind the spindle; 10 mm steel spokes with 25 mm black ball knobs 14 cm from the shaft; its pinion moves the quill 15 mm per radian (94 mm per turn); at rest the front spoke points 70 degrees forward of straight down. Motor: a no-volt-release push-button switch box (70 x 60 x 40 mm) on the front of the head, right of centre: a green 20 mm start button 2.2 cm and a red 28 mm stop button 5.8 cm right of the centre line, both 40 cm up, each pressing in 4 mm (switching at 2 mm, 4.8-7.2 N). The motor runs only when started there, whether or not the quill moves. (2) The drill's cast-iron table, 160 x 160 mm, set with its top 16 cm up, covered by a fixed spoil board: white melamine-faced MDF 10 mm thick, waxed, so parts slide and turn on it easily; a bit that goes through a part goes into it. (3) A loose aluminium plate, 130 x 150 x 10 mm, 0.53 kg, on the spoil board from 21.5 to 34.5 cm forward and from 8.5 cm right of the centre line to 6.5 cm left of it (its front 2.5 cm overhangs the board), with a black punch mark (a cross) on top under the bit, 2.5 cm from its back edge; the bit's tip is 5 mm above it. (4) A fixed hold-down screw clamp bolted to the table: a post left of the plate and an arm over its front-left part; its steel screw comes down through the arm 6.8 cm ahead of the spindle and 4 cm left of the centre line, with a black rubber pad 2 cm across 4 mm above the plate and a red plastic square knob 1.6 cm across on top, its top 25 cm up. Turning the knob clockwise (seen from above) drives the screw down 8 mm per turn; the pad turns with it. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial, with latches for what happens during it; each check is given with its simulation measurement and its real-trial measurement. Clamped: the pad on the plate with the knob turned at least a quarter turn (2 mm of screw travel) past the pad touching it (simulation: its soft screw spring presses 6 N there); real trial: the knob tightened to at least 0.4 N m, checked with a torque screwdriver (about 100 N at the pad). Drilled through at the mark: while the chuck turned and the plate was clamped, the bit's tip cut 11.5 mm below the plate's top (through the 10 mm plate and 1.5 mm into the spoil board), the hole within 5 mm of the mark; real trial: a 5 mm gauge pin passes through the hole and calipers put its centre within 5 mm of the punch mark. The chuck turns only after the green start button is pressed in past its 2 mm switch point, and runs down after the red stop button is. Unsafe: while the chuck turned faster than 1 rad/s, any point of either gripper's hand or wrist (both wrist links, the gripper body and both fingers, from their collision meshes) came within 5 cm of the bit or the chuck; real trial: judged frame by frame from the overhead and wrist videos with the 46 mm chuck as the scale. Spoilt (0.0): the turning bit met a plate that was not clamped (it is caught and flung; real trial: the plate spun or moved off its pencil outline), or the bit was pushed 0.5 mm into the plate while not turning (real trial: the quill pushed down onto the plate with the chuck stopped). Left safe: the quill within 3 mm of its top stop and the motor off with the chuck slower than 1 rad/s; real trial: the depth scale at 0, the switch off and the chuck still. 1.0: drilled through at the mark, never unsafe, and at the end the plate still clamped and the drill left safe; 0.5: never unsafe and either drilled through at the mark but the drill left running, its quill down or the clamp loosened, or the plate clamped with its mark within 5 mm of the bit's axis but not drilled through; 0.25: the plate clamped but off its mark, or drilled through or clamped but unsafe at some point; 0.0: otherwise, or spoilt. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the plate, the quill, the feed handle, the clamp's screw and the chuck still.
reset_notes: Press the red stop button and let the chuck stop; let the quill up; loosen the clamp to 4 mm above the plate; put a fresh undrilled plate on its pencil outline with the mark under the bit, over an undrilled spot of the spoil board.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). PhysX's gear joint does not run on the GPU, so the rack and pinion is two stiff drives re-aimed at each other every 1/240 s step (0.7 mm of give). The bit does not collide: drilling is judged from its tip, with the feed thrust as damping (50 N per mm/s), not the torque. The clamp's soft screw spring presses 6 N at a quarter turn (real about 100 N). The chuck turns at 180 rpm so the cameras show it (real 740-3140). Cameras 1280 x 704.
